gloss: A fuel such as coal, oil, or natural gas that formed underground over millions of years.
examples: Most of our electricity still comes from *fossil fuels*.
Coal is the dirtiest *fossil fuel* we burn.
The country wants to cut its use of *fossil fuels* in half.

gloss: Oil as it comes out of the ground, before it is refined.
examples: The price of *crude oil* jumped again this week.
The tanker was carrying two million barrels of *crude oil*.
*Crude oil* has to be refined before you can burn it in a car.

gloss: The thick dark oil pumped from underground that fuels and plastics are made from.
examples: Plastic is made from *petroleum*.
The company has been drilling for *petroleum* since the 1920s.
Almost every part of that engine runs on *petroleum* products.

gloss: A plant where crude oil is turned into gasoline, diesel, and other fuels.
examples: A fire shut the *refinery* down for two weeks.
There are three *refineries* along the coast.
He drove a truck between the *refinery* and the airport.

gloss: A thin oil burned in lamps, heaters, and jet engines.
examples: We filled the lamp with *kerosene* before the storm.
The cabin smelled faintly of *kerosene*.
*Kerosene* burns hotter than lamp oil.
contrast: Americans call it *kerosene*; the British say *paraffin*.

gloss: A gas stored under pressure in tanks and burned for cooking and heating.
examples: The grill ran out of *propane* halfway through dinner.
Their cabin is heated with *propane*.
*Propane* costs less than electricity out here.

gloss: A gas used in lighters and small camping stoves.
examples: The lighter takes a small can of *butane*.
Campers often cook on *butane* instead of wood.
*Butane* turns to liquid under very little pressure.

gloss: The main gas in natural gas, also released by landfills and cattle.
examples: The landfill captures *methane* and burns it for power.
*Methane* traps far more heat than carbon dioxide does.
Miners watched carefully for *methane* underground.
contrast: Americans say MEH-thayn; the British say MEE-thayn.

gloss: The gas piped into homes and power plants for heating and cooking.
examples: Our furnace runs on *natural gas*.
*Natural gas* is cheaper here than heating oil.
The plant switched from coal to *natural gas*.

gloss: Alcohol made from corn or sugar and blended into gasoline as fuel.
examples: Most gasoline here contains ten percent *ethanol*.
Iowa farmers grow a lot of corn for *ethanol*.
Older engines can be damaged by too much *ethanol*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Fuel made from plants, crops, or waste rather than from oil.
examples: The airline is testing a *biofuel* made from used cooking oil.
*Biofuels* still make up a small share of the market.
Their buses run on *biofuel* half the year.

gloss: The oil that keeps the moving parts of an engine lubricated.
examples: Check the *motor oil* before a long drive.
He bought five quarts of *motor oil* at the store.
Dirty *motor oil* will wear out an engine fast.

gloss: A heavy oil burned in ships, boilers, and industrial furnaces.
examples: The freighter burns heavy *fuel oil* at sea.
The plant keeps a month of *fuel oil* in storage.
New rules limit the sulfur in *fuel oil*.

gloss: Oil delivered to a house and burned in a furnace for warmth.
examples: *Heating oil* is expensive in New England this winter.
The truck comes twice a season to deliver *heating oil*.
We ran out of *heating oil* during the cold snap.

gloss: The refined kerosene that airplanes burn.
examples: *Jet fuel* prices drive up the cost of a ticket.
The plane took on forty thousand pounds of *jet fuel*.
A pipeline carries *jet fuel* straight to the airport.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: An oil or grease that lets moving parts slide without wearing out.
examples: The bearings need a heavier *lubricant* in summer.
The plant makes *lubricants* for heavy machinery.
A little *lubricant* on the chain will stop that noise.

gloss: A substance mixed into fuel or oil in small amounts to improve it.
examples: He poured a fuel *additive* into the tank.
These *additives* keep the engine cleaner.
The *additive* raises the octane a little.

gloss: A soft white wax made from petroleum and used in candles and sealing.
examples: Most cheap candles are made of *paraffin*.
She sealed the jars with melted *paraffin*.
*Paraffin* melts at a fairly low temperature.
contrast: In the US *paraffin* is wax; in Britain it means kerosene.

gloss: Wood cut and dried for burning.
examples: We stacked the *firewood* against the north wall.
He sells *firewood* by the cord every fall.
There is still plenty of *firewood* in the shed.

gloss: Small dry sticks used to start a fire.
examples: Grab some *kindling* from the porch.
The *kindling* was too damp to catch.
He split a few logs into *kindling*.

gloss: An iron stove that burns wood to heat a room.
examples: The cabin is heated by a single *wood stove*.
Old *wood stoves* put out a lot of smoke.
She fed another log into the *wood stove*.

gloss: Dark decayed plant matter dug from bogs and dried for fuel.
examples: They still burn *peat* in parts of Ireland.
The bog has been cut for *peat* for generations.
*Peat* smoke gives the whisky its flavor.

gloss: A small hard lump of compressed material such as sawdust burned as fuel.
examples: The stove burns wood *pellets* instead of logs.
A forty-pound bag of *pellets* lasts about two days.
Each *pellet* is about the size of a grain of rice.

gloss: A plastic or metal container for carrying gasoline.
examples: There is a red *gas can* in the garage.
He walked two miles with an empty *gas can*.
Keep the *gas cans* away from the water heater.

gloss: The container that holds the fuel a vehicle or machine runs on.
examples: The *fuel tank* holds about twenty gallons.
Rust had eaten a hole in the *fuel tank*.
Both *fuel tanks* were nearly empty.

gloss: A steel cylinder that holds propane under pressure.
examples: I need to swap out the *propane tank* for the grill.
The *propane tanks* are stored behind the store.
A full *propane tank* is heavy enough to need two hands.

gloss: A small flame that burns all the time and lights a gas appliance when it turns on.
examples: The *pilot light* on the furnace went out again.
You have to relight the *pilot light* by hand.
Newer heaters do not have *pilot lights* at all.

gloss: An area of ground with oil underneath it that is being pumped out.
examples: He spent ten years working in the *oil fields*.
The *oil field* is nearly played out.
A new *oil field* was found off the coast.

gloss: A deep hole drilled into the ground to bring up oil, gas, or water.
examples: The company drilled a new *well* last spring.
Several *wells* in the county have run dry.
They capped the *well* after the leak.

gloss: The tall structure and machinery used to drill for oil.
examples: His brother works two weeks on, two weeks off on an *oil rig*.
You can see the *oil rigs* from the beach.
A storm forced them to evacuate the *oil rig*.

gloss: The work of boring deep holes into the ground to reach oil, gas, or water.
examples: *Drilling* began in March and finished in July.
The state banned *drilling* near the reservoir.
Offshore *drilling* costs far more than drilling on land.

gloss: A method of forcing gas and oil out of rock by pumping liquid into it at high pressure.
examples: *Fracking* transformed the gas industry in Pennsylvania.
Neighbors worry that *fracking* is polluting their wells.
The town voted to ban *fracking* inside city limits.

gloss: An accidental release of oil into the sea or onto land.
examples: The *oil spill* killed thousands of seabirds.
Cleaning up the *oil spill* took three years.
Big *oil spills* are rarer now than they used to be.

gloss: A very large ship built to carry oil.
examples: An *oil tanker* was waiting outside the harbor.
The biggest *oil tankers* are longer than three football fields.
The *oil tanker* ran aground in heavy fog.

gloss: A place where coal is dug out of the ground.
examples: His grandfather worked in a *coal mine* for thirty years.
Most of the *coal mines* around here closed in the eighties.
The *coal mine* employs four hundred people.

gloss: Someone whose job is digging coal, ore, or minerals out of the ground.
examples: The *miners* came up covered in black dust.
A retired *miner* showed us around the old shaft.
Thirty *miners* were trapped for two days.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *minor*, meaning small or under eighteen.

gloss: The industry of taking coal, metal, or minerals out of the earth.
examples: *Mining* was the only industry in that valley.
She studies the effects of *mining* on rivers.
Copper *mining* still pays well in Arizona.

gloss: A deep vertical passage cut down into a mine.
examples: The *shaft* goes down almost a thousand feet.
Both *shafts* were sealed after the accident.
An elevator carries the crew down the *shaft*.

gloss: An open pit where stone, sand, or gravel is cut or dug out.
examples: The limestone came from a *quarry* upstate.
Two old *quarries* have filled with water.
Trucks leave the *quarry* every few minutes.

gloss: A mine where the soil above the coal is stripped off instead of tunneling.
examples: A *strip mine* took the whole side of the hill.
*Strip mines* are cheaper to run than deep mines.
The company has to restore the land after the *strip mine* closes.

gloss: Rock that contains enough metal to be worth mining.
examples: The train hauls iron *ore* to the mill.
This *ore* is about two percent copper.
They crush the *ore* before smelting it.
contrast: Sounds like *oar* and, for most Americans, like *or*.

gloss: The fine black powder produced when coal is cut or handled.
examples: *Coal dust* covered every window in town.
Years of breathing *coal dust* ruined his lungs.
A spark in the *coal dust* can set off an explosion.

gloss: A large machine with a bucket on an arm for digging earth.
examples: An *excavator* dug the foundation in a single day.
Two *excavators* were loading trucks at the pit.
He has driven an *excavator* since he was twenty.

gloss: The process of taking a resource such as oil or metal out of the ground.
examples: Oil *extraction* uses a huge amount of water.
The law taxes the *extraction* of coal and gas.
*Extraction* costs rise as the easy deposits run out.

gloss: A building or site where electricity is generated.
examples: The *power station* burns coal from a nearby mine.
Three *power stations* feed the city.
The old *power station* was torn down last year.
contrast: Americans usually say *power plant*; *power station* is more British.

gloss: A large tank that heats water into steam for heating or for driving a turbine.
examples: The *boiler* in the basement is forty years old.
Both *boilers* were shut down for cleaning.
Steam from the *boiler* spins the turbine.

gloss: A tall chimney that carries smoke away from a factory or power plant.
examples: You can see the *smokestacks* from the highway.
The *smokestack* is over three hundred feet tall.
They painted stripes on the *smokestack* to warn planes.

gloss: A wide curved tower that lets a power plant release waste heat as steam.
examples: Steam rose from the *cooling towers* all morning.
The plant has two concrete *cooling towers*.
That white cloud over the *cooling tower* is just water vapor.

gloss: A device that cools steam or gas back into a liquid.
examples: The *condenser* turns the used steam back into water.
A leak in the *condenser* cut the plant's output.
Both *condensers* are cooled with river water.

gloss: A long metal tube of nuclear fuel loaded into a reactor.
examples: The *fuel rods* are replaced every eighteen months.
A damaged *fuel rod* set off the alarm.
Spent *fuel rods* are stored under water for years.

gloss: An accident in which a nuclear reactor overheats and its core melts.
examples: The plant came within hours of a *meltdown*.
Two *meltdowns* have shaped how reactors are designed.
Backup pumps are there to prevent a *meltdown*.

gloss: Radioactive material left over from running a nuclear reactor.
examples: Nobody wants *nuclear waste* buried in their state.
The plant stores its *nuclear waste* on site.
*Nuclear waste* stays dangerous for thousands of years.
contrast: *Nuclear* has three syllables, NOO-klee-ur; NOO-kyuh-lur is a common error.

gloss: A heavy radioactive metal made in reactors and used in fuel and weapons.
examples: A few kilograms of *plutonium* are enough for a bomb.
The reactor produces *plutonium* as a byproduct.
Inspectors keep track of every gram of *plutonium*.

gloss: A building or tower with sails or blades turned by the wind.
examples: An old *windmill* pumps water for the cattle.
The hillside is dotted with *windmills*.
The *windmill* has not turned in years.

gloss: A tall tower with long blades that turns wind into electricity.
examples: A single *wind turbine* can power hundreds of homes.
The *wind turbines* were shut down during the storm.
They are building a *wind turbine* on the ridge.

gloss: A group of wind turbines built together to generate electricity.
examples: The *wind farm* supplies power to three counties.
Offshore *wind farms* cost more to build.
You drive past the *wind farm* on the way to Amarillo.

gloss: A flat sheet mounted on a roof or frame that turns sunlight into electricity.
examples: We put *solar panels* on the garage roof.
One *solar panel* is not enough to run the house.
Snow on the *solar panels* cuts their output.

gloss: One small unit that produces electricity from light, many of which make a panel.
examples: Each panel holds sixty *solar cells*.
A cracked *solar cell* can pull down the whole panel.
The calculator runs off a tiny *solar cell*.

gloss: Electricity produced from sunlight.
examples: The school runs almost entirely on *solar power*.
*Solar power* has gotten much cheaper in ten years.
They rely on *solar power* and a backup generator.

gloss: A large field of solar panels that feeds electricity into the grid.
examples: A *solar farm* now covers the old airfield.
Two *solar farms* were approved this year.
The *solar farm* takes up four hundred acres.

gloss: Electricity generated by moving water.
examples: The Northwest gets most of its electricity from *hydropower*.
*Hydropower* depends on how much snow falls in the mountains.
The dam has produced *hydropower* since 1938.

gloss: Plant material and waste burned or processed to make energy.
examples: The plant burns *biomass* left over from logging.
*Biomass* supplies a small share of the state's power.
They tested wood chips and other *biomass* as fuel.

gloss: The unit that feeds a machine the electricity it needs.
examples: The *power supply* burned out and killed the computer.
Bring a spare *power supply* to the site.
Both *power supplies* are rated for the same voltage.

gloss: The network of lines and stations that carries electricity across a region.
examples: The heat wave pushed the *grid* to its limit.
Their cabin is off the *grid* entirely.
Texas runs its own *grid*, separate from the rest of the country.

gloss: A company that supplies electricity, gas, or water to the public.
examples: The *utility* asked customers to cut back during the heat wave.
Several *utilities* raised their rates in January.
He worked for the local *utility* for thirty years.

gloss: A wooden post along a street that carries power and phone lines.
examples: The car slid off the road and hit a *utility pole*.
Crews replaced twelve *utility poles* after the storm.
Someone stapled a lost dog notice to the *utility pole*.

gloss: A high-voltage line that carries electricity long distances.
examples: A new *transmission line* will connect the wind farm to the city.
*Transmission lines* cross the valley on steel towers.
Ice brought down the *transmission line* in two places.

gloss: A fenced site where the voltage of electricity is changed before it goes on.
examples: A fire at the *substation* left the town dark.
There are two *substations* on the edge of town.
The *substation* steps the voltage down for local streets.

gloss: A unit of power equal to a million watts.
examples: The plant produces six hundred *megawatts*.
One *megawatt* is roughly enough for several hundred homes.
They added fifty *megawatts* of solar last year.

gloss: A switch that cuts off the current automatically when a circuit is overloaded.
examples: The *circuit breaker* tripped when I ran the heater.
Flip the *circuit breaker* back on in the basement.
Half the *circuit breakers* in that panel are mislabeled.

gloss: The metal box in a building that holds the fuses or breakers for its circuits.
examples: The *fuse box* is behind the door in the hallway.
Old houses often still have a *fuse box*.
He checked both *fuse boxes* before calling an electrician.

gloss: A period when the electricity fails across a whole area.
examples: The *blackout* left half the state without power.
Rolling *blackouts* began in the afternoon.
We kept candles in the drawer after that *blackout*.

gloss: A period when the power or another service stops working.
examples: The *outage* lasted about six hours.
Storms caused *outages* in three counties.
Call the utility to report an *outage*.

gloss: A drop in voltage that dims the lights without cutting the power off.
examples: A *brownout* made the lights flicker all evening.
*Brownouts* are common when everyone runs the air conditioning.
The *brownout* damaged the motor on the freezer.

gloss: A sudden jump in electric current or voltage that can damage equipment.
examples: A *surge* from the lightning strike fried the router.
*Surges* are common when the power comes back on.
The *surge* blew out three bulbs at once.

gloss: A device that shields plugged-in equipment from sudden jumps in voltage.
examples: Plug the computer into a *surge protector*.
Cheap *surge protectors* wear out after a few years.
The *surge protector* took the hit instead of the TV.

gloss: A bar of electrical outlets on a cord.
examples: Everything under the desk runs off one *power strip*.
Do not plug a heater into a *power strip*.
We need two more *power strips* for the office.

gloss: A sudden painful jolt caused by electricity passing through the body.
examples: He got a *shock* from the frayed cord.
Wet hands make a *shock* much more dangerous.
She felt small *shocks* every time she touched the railing.

gloss: A fault in which current takes a wrong path and flows where it should not.
examples: A *short circuit* in the wiring started the fire.
The mechanic traced the *short circuit* to a pinched wire.
*Short circuits* usually trip the breaker right away.

gloss: More current or weight on a system than it is built to handle.
examples: The fuse blew because of an *overload*.
Repeated *overloads* will ruin the motor.
An *overload* on the grid caused the outage.
contrast: The noun is stressed OH-vur-lohd; the verb is oh-vur-LOHD.

gloss: A wire that is carrying electric current.
examples: A *live wire* was lying across the driveway.
Never touch a *live wire* with bare hands.
Crews cordoned off the *live wires* after the crash.
contrast: Here *live* rhymes with *five*, not with *give*.

gloss: A metal piece through which current enters or leaves a battery, cell, or welder.
examples: The welder replaced a burned *electrode*.
Both *electrodes* were coated with a white residue.
Current flows from one *electrode* to the other.

gloss: Wire wound into loops so that it makes or responds to a magnetic field.
examples: The *coil* in the ignition had gone bad.
Copper *coils* surround the iron core.
Heat from the *coil* warms the water.

gloss: A small part that stores electric charge and releases it quickly.
examples: A blown *capacitor* kept the motor from starting.
The board is covered in tiny *capacitors*.
Discharge the *capacitor* before you touch anything.

gloss: A device that changes direct current from a battery or panel into household current.
examples: The solar panels feed an *inverter* in the garage.
A small *inverter* lets you run a laptop off the car.
Both *inverters* failed in the same month.

gloss: A pipe or tube that protects electrical wiring.
examples: The wiring runs through metal *conduit* along the wall.
They buried two *conduits* under the driveway.
Code requires *conduit* in a garage.

gloss: A place where an electric vehicle can be plugged in and recharged.
examples: There is a *charging station* behind the grocery store.
New *charging stations* are going in along the interstate.
We waited twenty minutes for a free *charging station*.

gloss: A set of batteries joined together to power a vehicle or tool.
examples: The *battery pack* sits under the floor of the car.
Replacement *battery packs* are expensive.
A cold morning cuts the range of the *battery pack*.

gloss: A statement of what you owe for electricity, gas, or water.
examples: Our *utility bill* doubled in January.
He pays all the *utility bills* online.
Bring a *utility bill* as proof of address.

gloss: The amount of energy, fuel, or goods that is used up.
examples: Electricity *consumption* peaks on hot afternoons.
New insulation cut our *consumption* by a third.
The country's oil *consumption* has been flat for a decade.

gloss: How much useful work a machine or building gets out of the energy it uses.
examples: The new boiler improved *efficiency* by fifteen percent.
Energy *efficiency* saves more than new power plants do.
*Efficiency* drops sharply when the filters are dirty.

gloss: A gas or particle released into the air by burning fuel.
examples: The plant cut its *emissions* by half.
Carbon *emissions* rose again last year.
Every *emission* from the stack is measured.

gloss: A gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide or methane.
examples: Burning coal releases a lot of *greenhouse gas*.
Methane is a far stronger *greenhouse gas* than carbon dioxide.
The law caps *greenhouse gases* from power plants.
contrast: The plural is *gases* with one s; *gasses* is the verb form.

gloss: The gas released whenever carbon fuels are burned.
examples: The plant puts out millions of tons of *carbon dioxide* a year.
Trees take in *carbon dioxide* and give off oxygen.
They are testing a way to capture *carbon dioxide* at the stack.

gloss: Rain made acidic by pollution from burning coal and oil.
examples: *Acid rain* killed the fish in hundreds of lakes.
Scrubbers on the smokestacks reduced *acid rain*.
*Acid rain* ate away at the stone carvings.

gloss: The steady rise in the earth's temperature caused mainly by burning fuel.
examples: *Global warming* is already changing growing seasons.
Coal plants are a major cause of *global warming*.
Scientists warned about *global warming* decades ago.

gloss: Long-term shifts in weather patterns caused largely by greenhouse gases.
examples: *Climate change* was the main issue in the debate.
The utility says it is planning for *climate change*.
Insurers are raising rates because of *climate change*.

gloss: The practice of using less of a resource so that it lasts longer.
examples: Energy *conservation* is cheaper than building new plants.
The city put out a *conservation* notice during the drought.
Simple *conservation* measures cut the bill right away.

gloss: Material left over from a process that is thrown away.
examples: The mill produces tons of *waste* every day.
Industrial *waste* used to go straight into the river.
Some of the *waste* is burned for heat.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *waist*, the middle of the body.

gloss: Dirty water left over from an industrial process or from homes.
examples: The plant treats its own *wastewater* before releasing it.
*Wastewater* from the mine leaked into the creek.
Pipes carry the *wastewater* to a holding pond.

gloss: Something produced along the way while making something else.
examples: Sulfur is a *byproduct* of refining oil.
The mill sells its *byproducts* to a cement plant.
Heat is an unavoidable *byproduct* of generating power.

gloss: The stony waste that floats off metal during smelting.
examples: Piles of *slag* still sit beside the old mill.
They pour the *slag* off before tapping the iron.
Some *slag* is crushed and used in road building.

gloss: A factory where a raw material such as steel, paper, or grain is processed.
examples: Half the town worked at the *mill*.
The paper *mill* closed in 2004.
Two *mills* along the river are still running.

gloss: A large plant where steel is made and rolled into shape.
examples: The *steel mill* ran three shifts a day.
Most of the *steel mills* around Pittsburgh are gone.
He got a job at the *steel mill* right out of high school.

gloss: A workshop where metal is melted and poured into molds.
examples: The *foundry* casts engine blocks.
It is a hundred degrees inside the *foundry* in July.
Small *foundries* have trouble competing on price.

gloss: A plant where metal is separated from ore by heat.
examples: The copper *smelter* is the biggest employer in the county.
Fumes from the *smelter* damaged nearby crops.
Two *smelters* shut down when the price of metal fell.

gloss: A tall furnace that blows hot air through ore and coke to make iron.
examples: The *blast furnace* runs day and night.
They shut down the second *blast furnace* in 2019.
Molten iron pours out of the *blast furnace* into a ladle.

gloss: A line of workers and machines that put a product together piece by piece.
examples: She spent twenty years on the *assembly line*.
A single broken robot stopped the whole *assembly line*.
Both *assembly lines* build the same model.

gloss: A moving band that carries parts or goods through a factory.
examples: Boxes ride down the *conveyor belt* to the loading dock.
The *conveyor belt* jammed and shut the line down.
Long *conveyor belts* carry coal to the power plant.

gloss: The area of a factory where the actual work is done.
examples: The new manager spends every morning on the *shop floor*.
Nobody on the *shop floor* was told about the merger.
Safety glasses are required on the *shop floor*.

gloss: The making of goods in large quantities.
examples: *Production* fell sharply after the strike.
The plant will start *production* in the fall.
They moved *production* to another state.

gloss: The industry of making goods in factories.
examples: *Manufacturing* still employs thousands here.
He works in *manufacturing*, not in sales.
The town lost most of its *manufacturing* in the nineties.

gloss: How much a worker or a plant produces in a given amount of time.
examples: The new machines raised *productivity* by a fifth.
*Productivity* dropped on the night shift.
Managers track *productivity* line by line.

gloss: The joining of metal pieces by melting them together.
examples: He learned *welding* at a trade school.
The *welding* on that frame is sloppy.
*Welding* throws off sparks and hard ultraviolet light.

gloss: A worker who joins metal by melting it, or the machine used to do it.
examples: A good *welder* can name his own price right now.
The shop hired three more *welders*.
He bought a small *welder* for the garage.

gloss: The joint where two pieces of metal have been melted together.
examples: The *weld* cracked under load.
An inspector x-rayed every *weld* on the pipeline.
Those *welds* look clean and even.

gloss: A skilled worker who shapes metal parts on machine tools.
examples: The *machinist* cut the part to within a thousandth of an inch.
Good *machinists* are hard to find.
She trained as a *machinist* after the mill closed.

gloss: Someone whose job is running a machine or a plant.
examples: The crane *operator* has been here longer than anyone.
Two *operators* watch the control room around the clock.
Every *operator* has to be certified.

gloss: A worker who supervises a crew on a job or in a plant.
examples: The *foreman* sent everyone home early.
All the *foremen* meet on Monday mornings.
He worked his way up to *foreman* in six years.
contrast: The plural is *foremen*, not *foremans*.

gloss: A worker who does heavy physical work that needs no special training.
examples: He started as a *laborer* and ended up running the plant.
The contractor hired twenty *laborers* for the shutdown.
A *laborer* here earns more than a clerk downtown.
contrast: American spelling *laborer*; the British write *labourer*.

gloss: Physical work, or the workers who do it, considered as a whole.
examples: *Labor* costs more than materials on this job.
Cheap *labor* drew the factories overseas.
The dispute between *labor* and management dragged on for months.
contrast: American spelling *labor*; the British write *labour*.

gloss: All the people employed by a company or available to work in an area.
examples: The plant cut its *workforce* by a third.
Half the *workforce* is over fifty.
The region has a skilled *workforce* and cheap power.

gloss: Someone learning a skilled trade by working under an experienced worker.
examples: He spent four years as an *apprentice* electrician.
The union takes on a dozen *apprentices* each spring.
An *apprentice* earns less but learns on the job.

gloss: Money paid to a worker, usually by the hour or the week.
examples: *Wages* at the plant have not risen in three years.
The union is asking for a higher *wage*.
He spent his whole *wage* on rent.

gloss: A rigid helmet worn to protect the head on a job site.
examples: You cannot go past that line without a *hard hat*.
There are spare *hard hats* by the door.
His *hard hat* was covered in stickers.

gloss: A small soft plug worn in the ear to block loud noise.
examples: *Earplugs* are required anywhere near the press.
He forgot his *earplugs* and had a headache all day.
A box of foam *earplugs* sits by the entrance.

gloss: Protection from harm, especially the rules and habits that prevent accidents at work.
examples: *Safety* comes before production on this site.
The plant has a strong *safety* record.
Every shift starts with a short *safety* meeting.

gloss: Something that could cause injury or damage.
examples: Loose cable on the floor is a tripping *hazard*.
Inspectors listed a dozen *hazards* in the report.
Coal dust is a serious fire *hazard*.

gloss: A careful official check of equipment or a workplace.
examples: The boiler failed its annual *inspection*.
Surprise *inspections* keep everyone honest.
The *inspection* turned up a cracked valve.

gloss: A fault in a product that makes it fail to meet the standard.
examples: The whole batch had the same *defect*.
Inspectors found three *defects* in the casting.
A tiny *defect* in the weld caused the failure.
contrast: The noun is stressed DEE-fekt; the verb *defect* is dih-FEKT.

gloss: Waste metal or material that is collected to be melted down and reused.
examples: They sold the old machines for *scrap*.
The mill buys *scrap* by the ton.
There is a pile of *scrap* behind the shop.

gloss: A fixed amount that must be produced or is allowed to be produced.
examples: The crew hit its *quota* by Thursday.
Production *quotas* were raised again this quarter.
Missing the *quota* two months running cost him the job.

gloss: The stock of goods and materials a business is holding.
examples: The plant is carrying too much *inventory*.
They cut *inventory* to free up cash.
Parts sat in *inventory* for eight months.
contrast: Americans say IN-vuhn-tor-ee; the British say in-VEN-tuh-ree.

gloss: A basic substance that a factory turns into a finished product.
examples: The price of *raw materials* went up sharply.
Iron ore is the main *raw material* for steel.
They store the *raw materials* in silos out back.

gloss: One of the parts that a machine or product is built from.
examples: A single *component* held up the whole order.
Most of the *components* come from three suppliers.
They test every *component* before assembly.

gloss: A part with balls or rollers that lets a shaft turn smoothly.
examples: A worn *bearing* was making that whine.
The *bearings* need grease every hundred hours.
He pressed a new *bearing* onto the shaft.

gloss: A machine that squeezes air or gas into a smaller space under pressure.
examples: The *compressor* kicks on every few minutes.
Both *compressors* feed the same air line.
A leak upstream kept the *compressor* running all night.

gloss: A case of gears that changes the speed or force coming from a motor.
examples: Oil was leaking out of the *gearbox*.
The *gearbox* on the wind turbine failed after eight years.
They rebuilt both *gearboxes* over the weekend.

gloss: A pipe or channel that carries air, gas, or fumes through a building.
examples: Warm air comes up through the *duct* in the floor.
The *ducts* had not been cleaned in years.
A steel *duct* carries the fumes to the roof.

gloss: The pipe or passage that carries smoke and hot gas out of a furnace.
examples: Open the *flue* before you light the fire.
Soot had nearly blocked the *flue*.
Both *flues* run up the same chimney.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *flu* and *flew*.

gloss: The movement of fresh air through a building or a mine.
examples: The mine has *ventilation* shafts every half mile.
Poor *ventilation* let the fumes build up.
They installed better *ventilation* over the welding bays.

gloss: A device that keeps pressure, voltage, or flow at a steady level.
examples: The *regulator* on the propane tank was frozen.
A bad *regulator* let the voltage swing wildly.
Both *regulators* were replaced during the overhaul.

gloss: A machine with a chain or cable for lifting heavy loads.
examples: They lifted the motor out with a chain *hoist*.
The *hoist* is rated for two tons.
Both *hoists* run on the same overhead rail.

gloss: A low wooden platform that goods are stacked on so a forklift can move them.
examples: Stack the boxes on a *pallet* and shrink-wrap them.
There are forty *pallets* waiting at the dock.
A broken *pallet* dumped the whole load.
contrast: Sounds like *palette*, the painter's board, and like *palate*, the roof of the mouth.

gloss: A large wooden or plastic box used for shipping goods.
examples: The machine arrived in a wooden *crate*.
Empty *crates* were stacked along the wall.
It took four men to move that *crate*.

gloss: A raised platform where trucks back up to be loaded or unloaded.
examples: Two trucks were waiting at the *loading dock*.
The *loading docks* run along the back of the building.
Drivers check in at the *loading dock* office.

gloss: Goods carried in bulk by truck, train, or ship.
examples: *Freight* moves through this yard day and night.
The cost of *freight* has doubled since spring.
Most of the coal travels as rail *freight*.
contrast: The *eigh* sounds like *ay*; the word rhymes with *eight*.

gloss: A load of goods sent out together.
examples: The *shipment* is due Thursday morning.
Three *shipments* were held up at the border.
We rejected the whole *shipment* after testing it.

gloss: The whole chain of suppliers and shippers that gets parts to a factory.
examples: One missing chip broke the entire *supply chain*.
Companies are shortening their *supply chains*.
The war disrupted the *supply chain* for months.

gloss: A building where goods, fuel, or vehicles are stored.
examples: The fuel *depot* sits just outside town.
Buses are serviced at the *depot* overnight.
Two *depots* supply the whole northern route.
contrast: The *t* is silent; Americans say DEE-poh, the British DEP-oh.

gloss: One part of an economy or industry considered separately.
examples: The energy *sector* added jobs last quarter.
Both *sectors* depend on cheap electricity.
Manufacturing is the largest *sector* in this county.

gloss: A complete repair in which a machine is taken apart and rebuilt.
examples: The turbine is due for an *overhaul* this fall.
Two *overhauls* are scheduled for the shutdown.
A full *overhaul* takes about six weeks.
contrast: The noun is stressed OH-vur-hawl; the verb is oh-vur-HAWL.

gloss: Work done to fix something that is broken or worn.
examples: The *repair* took longer than anyone expected.
Crews made emergency *repairs* to the line.
That *repair* will cost more than the pump is worth.

gloss: A hole or crack that lets liquid or gas escape.
examples: A gas *leak* forced them to clear the building.
Crews found two *leaks* in the pipeline.
The *leak* was losing a gallon an hour.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *leek*, the vegetable.

gloss: An accidental release of liquid onto the ground or into water.
examples: A chemical *spill* closed the highway.
Small *spills* have to be reported too.
They contained the *spill* within an hour.

gloss: The keeping of fuel, energy, or goods until they are needed.
examples: Battery *storage* lets the grid save solar power for evening.
The gas is kept in underground *storage* over the summer.
They rented extra *storage* for the spare parts.
